bull_thesis: The event this position was bought for has already happened, and it went the company's way. On 14 July 2026 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted full approval to REVTORPYK (gedatolisib), three days ahead of its own 17 July deadline, for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in patients without a PIK3CA mutation who have progressed on at least one line of hormone therapy. So the bull case is no longer about the ruling. It is about the fact that the market is now paying about 46% less for the company than it did before the ruling it was waiting for came in favourably. The label is genuinely strong. In the pivotal VIKTORIA-1 trial the three-drug regimen held the cancer in check for a median of 9.3 months against 2.0 months on fulvestrant alone (a hazard ratio of 0.24, meaning a 76% reduction in the risk of the disease worsening), with a 32% response rate and responses lasting a median of 17.5 months; the two-drug regimen delivered 7.4 months (hazard ratio 0.33) and a 28% response rate. Crucially this is full approval, not the conditional kind, so there is no confirmatory-trial obligation that could later unwind the label. Celcuity now owns the only approved drug that blocks all four class I PI3K enzymes together with both forms of mTOR, and it serves roughly 37,000 U.S. patients a year who, until two weeks ago, had no targeted option in this pathway at all. A second, larger patient group is queued behind it. In the mutated-gene arm of the same trial, reported 2 June 2026, gedatolisib beat Novartis's alpelisib head-to-head - 11.1 and 11.3 months against 5.6, response rates of 48.9% and 35.7% against 26.0% - and did so with far less of the high blood sugar that has held this drug class back commercially (11.5 to 15.0% of patients versus 57.9%), with fewer patients stopping treatment for side effects (2.6 to 3.8% versus 7.1%). A supplemental filing for that population is guided to the third quarter of 2026. Financing risk is essentially gone. The June 2026 sale of $500M of 0.250% convertible bonds due 2032, upsized from a planned $400M, brought in roughly $484M net, retired the expensive Oxford Finance secured loan in full, issued no stock, and leaves about $625M to $640M of cash with nothing to repay before 2032 - against a burn rate of roughly $52M a quarter. And the sell side has not left: after the approval, the consensus target is $155.11 with a median of $157, a high of $178 and a low of $110. Every published target sits above the $82.27 close of 27 July 2026. For the bull case to pay, three conditions must hold: the launch must actually start in late third quarter 2026 as guided rather than slipping again; real-world oncologists must tolerate a regimen that produced mouth sores in 58 to 72% of trial patients; and the supplemental filing for the mutated-gene group must be submitted, accepted, and eventually approved into a market that already contains alpelisib and capivasertib and will soon contain Relay Therapeutics' zovegalisib.
bear_thesis: The bear case is simply that the stock has already told us the answer. Celcuity has delivered three pieces of objectively good news this year - a head-to-head win over alpelisib on 2 June, a fully funded balance sheet on 3 June, and an early approval on 14 July - and the shares fell on all three, by about 25%, and then by 17.6% in a single session on 15 July. That is the signature of a crowded position unwinding after the event it was assembled for. The decision was fully priced at $151.02; it is not going to be paid for twice. The proximate damage came from management's own guidance. On the approval call they told the market that the U.S. launch would come 'late' in the third quarter of 2026, citing the need to build enough drug supply. The street had assumed something faster - Stifel called the guidance 'somewhat extended' - and the stock lost $19.54 to close at $91.51. Within nine days at least four plaintiffs' firms (Pomerantz, Bragar Eagel & Squire, Kirby McInerney, and Bronstein Gewirtz & Grossman) opened investigations into whether earlier disclosures about launch readiness were adequate. Those are investigations, not filed claims, and firms open them reflexively after any sharp drop - but they mark the size of the gap between what management let investors assume and what management delivered. This is the second such gap this year; the June data also undershot what the company's own earlier trial had conditioned investors to expect. The commercial risk is real and specific. Mouth sores affected 72% of patients on the three-drug regimen and 58% on the two-drug regimen, severe in 22% and 12% respectively, requiring a preventive steroid mouthwash; rash affected 30 to 40%. Trial protocols manage that. Community oncology practices often do not, and they may default to the weaker two-drug regimen or to nothing at all. Reuters named tolerability alongside the launch delay as the reason the stock fell, so this is not a theoretical concern. Underneath it there is no support. Cash of roughly $625M to $640M against $500M of convertible debt is net cash of about $140M, or roughly $3 a share on about 48.8 million shares, against a price of $82.27. There is no acquirer under contract, no contingent payment right, no recovery value - nothing that mechanically catches the price. This is a single-product, single-indication, single-pathway company that has never booked a dollar of product revenue, and the next hard information about whether any of this works is a revenue line in early November 2026. If the launch slips again, or if prescriptions come in soft, there is a long way down before anything structural stops it.
sop_bull: About $150 to $157 a share, and the parts are simple because there is only one drug. Part one, the approved wild-type indication: roughly 37,000 addressable U.S. patients a year; assume the drug reaches 20 to 25% of them at maturity at oncology pricing, held for 12 to 14 months on average, which supports peak annual U.S. net sales of about $1.3B to $1.6B. Part two, the mutated-gene expansion: filed in the third quarter of 2026, approved during 2027, contributing an incremental $0.8B to $1.0B of peak sales given the head-to-head win over alpelisib and the much cleaner blood-sugar profile, discounted for the arrival of Relay's zovegalisib and the existing presence of capivasertib. Part three, rights outside the United States, whether partnered or self-commercialised, worth perhaps $0.3B to $0.5B in present value. Total peak sales of roughly $2.2B to $2.6B; commercial-stage oncology companies with a differentiated single asset and a clear label-expansion path trade at roughly 3.0 to 3.5 times peak sales on an enterprise basis, giving $6.6B to $9.1B. Add cash of about $640M, subtract the $500M convertible, and divide by roughly 52 million fully diluted shares: $130 to $177 a share, centring near $153. That reconciles closely with the post-approval sell-side consensus of $155.11 and a median of $157, which is a useful cross-check rather than an independent confirmation.
sop_bear: About $50 to $55 a share - and it is important to be honest that this is a modelled adverse value, not a floor. There is nothing here that mechanically catches the price. The adverse path: the launch slips past late third quarter 2026; mouth sores in 58 to 72% of patients cap real-world uptake and push prescribers toward the weaker two-drug regimen; the mutated-gene expansion lands into a market already served by alpelisib and capivasertib with Relay's zovegalisib arriving, so it adds little. Peak annual sales settle around $1.0B to $1.2B rather than $2.2B or more. At two to two-and-a-half times peak sales on an enterprise basis that is $2.4B to $2.8B, plus $640M cash, less $500M of convertible debt, over about 49 million shares - roughly $50 to $58 a share. The board entry carried a $60 floor. That figure does not survive inspection as a floor: at $60 the enterprise is worth about $2.79B, which already requires peak sales above $1.2B, so it assumes the launch broadly works. It is a bear valuation, not a backstop. Below that estimate there is only the balance sheet: net cash of about $140M, or roughly $3 a share. A genuinely failed launch - peak sales of $600M to $800M - would imply something in the $30 to $40 range, and there is no contractual mechanism to prevent it. The one genuine cushion is not a number but an option: an approved, differentiated, fully funded oncology asset with a full (not conditional) label is a plausible acquisition target, and a strategic buyer would almost certainly pay well above net cash. That is optionality, not a floor.
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across the three commercial paths, because the regulatory question is already settled and only execution remains. (1) Launch lands on time and the mutated-gene expansion is approved during 2027 - the full sum-of-the-parts of about $153 a share, which we put at roughly 40% likely. (2) A workable but unspectacular launch, with tolerability capping uptake and the expansion arriving into competition - about $100 a share, roughly 35% likely. (3) The launch stumbles, whether on supply, another timing slip, or prescriber resistance to the mouth-sore burden - about $55 a share, roughly 25% likely. Weighted: 0.40 x $153 + 0.35 x $100 + 0.25 x $55 = about $110 a share. Cross-check on the components: at $110 the equity is about $5.4B and the enterprise about $5.2B, or roughly 2.9 times a $1.8B blended peak-sales estimate - a reasonable multiple for a differentiated commercial-stage oncology asset, and comfortably below the 3.0 to 3.5 times the bull case needs. Net cash contributes only about $3 a share; essentially all of the value is the drug.
risk_reward: About 2.6 to 1 measured against the modelled adverse value, but the denominator is soft. From $82.27, the upside to the event-resolved target of $153 is about +86%; the downside to a defensible adverse value of $55 is about -33%. Against the reconciled base case of $110 the upside is about +34%. The important qualification is that the -33% is not bounded. Unlike a merger with a signed agreement or a company trading near its cash, nothing here mechanically catches the price. A genuinely failed launch implies $30 to $40, which would make the real ratio closer to 1.7 to 1. So the honest statement is: a favourable ratio on the central case, over an open-ended tail.
catalyst_summary: The FDA approved REVTORPYK on 14 July 2026, three days ahead of the 17 July deadline - the catalyst has fired favourably and the stock fell 17.6% the next day on a launch pushed to late third quarter; from $82.27 the residual asymmetry is about +86% to a $153 target against roughly -33% to a $55 adverse value that is modelled rather than backstopped.
dated_milestone: The load-bearing event is already behind us: the FDA approved REVTORPYK (gedatolisib) on 14 July 2026, ahead of its 17 July 2026 decision date, verified against the company's release of that date and Reuters coverage of 15 July 2026. What remains is not dated in the binding sense - a supplemental filing for the PIK3CA-mutated population guided to the third quarter of 2026 (a company submission, not a regulator's decision), and a U.S. commercial launch guided to late in the third quarter of 2026 (a company-guided quarter that has already moved once relative to market expectations). The next genuinely fixed date is the third-quarter 2026 results report in early November 2026, which will carry the first REVTORPYK revenue line.
forcing_function: Three things, in order of how hard they are. The hardest is the third-quarter 2026 earnings report in early November 2026. That is a fixed reporting obligation and it will carry the first weeks of actual REVTORPYK prescriptions. This is the event that decides the stock, because it converts an argument about tolerability and prescriber willingness into a number. Second, acceptance of the supplemental filing for the mutated-gene population. The filing itself is guided to the third quarter of 2026; acceptance would set a new regulator's decision date roughly nine to twelve months out and restore a genuinely dated event to the story. That is the single development that could put this name back into an event-driven book. Third, and least reliable, the launch itself in late third quarter 2026 - a company-guided quarter that depends on supply readiness at a company that has never shipped a commercial product. It is as likely to disappoint again as to reassure. Note what is absent: there is no proxy contest, no strategic review, no activist, and no contractual deadline of any kind. The re-rating, if it comes, has to be earned with prescription data rather than forced by a calendar.
consensus_delta: There is a real disagreement here, but it does not point the way the position was originally sized to expect. Where the street is arguably wrong: every published price target sits above the current price - consensus $155.11, median $157, high $178, low $110 - and those were set or reaffirmed after the approval (H.C. Wainwright to $155, Citizens to $177, Stifel holding $175). The market is trading the stock at $82.27, roughly 47% below the consensus target. One of those two groups is wrong. The analysts are modelling a drug with a hazard ratio of 0.24 in a patient group of about 37,000 Americans a year who previously had no targeted option, sold by a company with $625M to $640M of cash and no debt maturity before 2032. The tape is pricing a company that cannot start selling for another five to nine weeks and has disappointed twice in two months. Where we disagree with the bulls: the sell-side targets rest on peak sales that require both a clean launch and the mutated-gene expansion, and they under-weight the tolerability question. Mouth sores in 72% of patients on the three-drug regimen, severe in 22%, requiring a preventive steroid mouthwash, is a real barrier in community oncology practice in a way it is not in a trial protocol. Models built on trial-derived treatment duration will overstate real-world duration if patients quit early. Where we disagree with the bears: the fall is being read as though something went wrong with the drug. Nothing did. The approval was full rather than conditional, it came early, and the label is broad. What went wrong was a communication about timing. Those are different failures with different half-lives. The honest position: the market and the street are arguing about launch execution, and neither of them has any data yet. Nobody does, until early November. That is not an information edge; it is a shared blind spot, and buying into a shared blind spot is not expectations arbitrage.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months are the hardest stretch this company will face, precisely because the good news is spent and the proof has not arrived. Cash is not the problem. The June convertible raise leaves roughly $625M to $640M against a burn of about $52M a quarter (the accumulated deficit moved from $448.9M at year-end 2025 to $501.7M at 31 March 2026), the expensive Oxford Finance secured loan is retired, and nothing is due before 2032. Even with commercial spending pushing quarterly burn toward $70M or $80M, there are years of runway. There is no maturity wall and no forced financing. The problem is a revenue vacuum with a full cost base. From the third quarter of 2026 Celcuity carries a sales force, a marketing organisation, and manufacturing commitments against nearly no revenue. Reported losses will get worse before they get better, and they will be reported against a company the market now labels commercial-stage. Three specific hazards sit inside the window. First, a second launch slip: 'late' third quarter is already a moving target tied to drug supply at a first-time commercial manufacturer, and a slip into the fourth quarter would be the second broken timing commitment in a quarter and would validate the plaintiffs' firms. Second, the early prescription data itself, arriving in the early-November third-quarter report - a soft first number is easy to explain away and impossible to un-see. Third, the tolerability question resolving badly in the real world: if community oncologists find the mouth-sore burden unmanageable and default to the weaker two-drug regimen or skip the drug entirely, that shows up as low refill rates roughly two quarters from now, which is exactly the window that matters. The legal overhang is a slower burn. Four investigations opened between 16 and 26 July 2026; if any converts into a filed class action it becomes a recurring headline and a disclosure constraint on management, without materially threatening the balance sheet.
positioning_washout: The washout is already well advanced, and that is the most interesting technical fact about this name. The shareholder base that assembled ahead of a regulatory decision is an event-driven base: biotech specialists and catalyst funds who size to a binary and exit on resolution regardless of which way it goes. That resolution came on 14 July. The exit is what has been happening since - a 17.6% single-day fall on 15 July to $91.51, roughly 15% over the following week, and a drift to $82.27 by 27 July. The stock now sits about 46% below its $151.02 high and below both its 50-day average of about $105 and its 200-day average of about $103, with daily volume around 1.3 million shares against roughly 48.8 million outstanding. Momentum and trend-following money is mechanically out once both moving averages break. What has not happened is the handoff. The natural next owners are the funds that buy commercial-stage oncology on prescription trends, and they have a reason to wait: there is no revenue line until early November. So the register is between owners, with the sellers largely done and the buyers not yet obliged to show up. That is a thin, unsupported tape - it cuts both ways, and it is why a modest positive surprise in November could move the stock hard. One structural detail worth flagging: the $500M convertible due 2032 means convertible-arbitrage desks now hold bonds and are short stock as a hedge. That short interest dampens rallies on the way up and cushions declines on the way down, and it is mechanical rather than opinionated. There is no dividend and no income-oriented holder base, so there is no yield-driven forced selling to come.
moderator_conclusion: This seat existed for one reason: a dated regulatory decision with a spread between the live price and the value the decision would unlock. That decision fired on 14 July 2026, three days early, and it went our way. The position is nonetheless down about 46% from the high. That single fact settles the question this funnel is meant to answer. The discipline here is not to be clever about it. A catalyst that has already resolved is spent, whichever way it resolved. The asymmetry we were paid to underwrite - a hard date, a binding decision, a bounded loss - no longer exists in this name. What remains is a commercial-launch story: whether a first-time commercial company can ship on time, whether oncologists will accept a regimen that produced mouth sores in 58 to 72% of trial patients, and whether a second label arrives before the competition does. Those are perfectly respectable questions. They are not event-driven questions, and they cannot be answered before the first revenue line arrives in early November 2026. The second finding is the one that decides the sizing. The downside floor of $60 carried on the board is not a floor. It is a bear valuation that already assumes the launch broadly works - at $60 the enterprise is worth about $2.79B, which needs peak annual sales above $1.2B. The only hard number underneath is net cash of roughly $140M, about $3 a share. There is no acquirer under contract, no contingent payment right, no recovery value. A defensible adverse case is $50 to $55, and a genuinely failed launch implies $30 to $40 with nothing structural in the way. Defined risk is the entire premise of this book, and the risk here is not defined. To be fair to the other side: the residual value case is not empty. At $82.27 against a reconciled base case of about $110, the stock is roughly 25% below fair value, the balance sheet is fixed through 2032, the approval is full rather than conditional, and every post-approval sell-side target - consensus $155.11, low $110 - sits above the price. Management delivered the approval early even as they mishandled the message about the launch. That is a real 25% discount on a real asset, which is why the value case scores in the middle of the range rather than lower. It is simply not a 25% discount with a floor under it. Verdict: pass for now, in this book. Not because the company is bad, and not because the drug disappointed - it did not. Because the event we were underwriting has happened, the spread closed in the wrong direction, and the loss is unbounded. If the Director wants exposure to Celcuity from here, it belongs in a growth or commercial-launch book at a size that survives a $40 print, not in a defined-risk event sleeve. The development that would bring it back into this funnel is specific: acceptance of the supplemental filing for the mutated-gene population, which would set a fresh regulator's decision date roughly nine to twelve months out and restore a genuinely dated event to the story. Watch for that, and watch the early-November revenue line.
interrogator_dossier:
# Celcuity Inc. (CELC) — Event Dossier

*Prepared 28 July 2026, re-verified against primary sources on that date. This is an
event-driven review, not a business-quality review. The question is not whether Celcuity is a
good company. The question is whether the event this position was bought for is still ahead of
us, and what actually catches the stock if things go wrong.*

**Headline finding: the event has already happened.** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration
approved Celcuity's lead drug on 14 July 2026, three days before its own deadline. The
approval went the company's way. The stock went the other way — it is down about 46% from its
52-week high of $151.02 and closed at $82.27 on 27 July 2026, below both its 50-day average of
about $105 and its 200-day average of about $103. Whatever the case for owning this name
today, it is no longer a case about a pending decision. It is a case about whether a
first-time commercial launch works.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Celcuity spent the last two years as a one-asset clinical company built around gedatolisib, a
drug that blocks all four class I PI3K enzymes plus both forms of mTOR — two linked switches
that tell breast-cancer cells to keep growing. The pitch was always that hitting the whole
pathway at once beats hitting one node of it.

The story moved in four steps this year, and the market's reaction got progressively worse at
each one even as the news got objectively better:

| Date | Event | Stock reaction |
|---|---|---|
| 20 Jan 2026 | FDA accepts the filing, grants priority review, sets a 17 July 2026 decision date | Positive; the run to $151.02 was built on this |
| 2 June 2026 | Detailed data in the mutated-gene group: the drug beats Novartis's alpelisib head-to-head | Fell about 25% — the result undershot an earlier trial |
| 3 June 2026 | Raises $500M of 0.250% convertible bonds due 2032, upsized from a planned $400M | Financing risk removed |
| 14 July 2026 | Approval granted, branded REVTORPYK, three days early | Fell 17.6% on 15 July, about 15% over the week |

That last line is the whole dossier. A company that gets an early approval on a first-in-class
drug and loses a sixth of its value in a week is telling you the decision was fully priced and
something in the follow-through was not.

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND STILL AHEAD? (the forensic core)

**It is real, it was dated, and it is spent.** On 14 July 2026 the FDA granted full approval —
not accelerated approval — for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic
breast cancer in patients without a PIK3CA mutation, after progression on at least one line of
hormone therapy. Full approval matters: there is no confirmatory-trial obligation hanging over
the label that could later be withdrawn.

The label itself is strong. In the pivotal VIKTORIA-1 trial the three-drug regimen held the
cancer in check for a median of 9.3 months versus 2.0 months on fulvestrant alone (hazard
ratio 0.24, a 76% reduction in the risk of the disease worsening), with a 32% response rate
and responses lasting a median of 17.5 months. The two-drug regimen delivered 7.4 months
(hazard ratio 0.33) with a 28% response rate. Those are not marginal numbers.

**What is left is not a catalyst in the sense this book uses the word.** Two things remain on
the calendar, and neither is a firm, third-party-enforced date:

- A supplemental filing for the mutated-gene population, guided to the third quarter of 2026.
  That is a submission by the company, not a decision by the regulator, and it is guided to a
  quarter rather than a day. Acceptance would then set a fresh decision date roughly nine to
  twelve months out.
- The U.S. commercial launch, guided to "late" in the third quarter of 2026, with management
  citing the need to build enough drug supply.

A company-guided quarter that has already moved once is a soft, non-binding milestone. It is
not the kind of firm scheduled event that forces a re-rating on a known day.

## 3. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR

Mixed, and the mix is the problem.

**On execution, management earned marks.** They filed on time, won priority review, and got
approved three days ahead of the deadline. They also solved the money problem before they had
to: the June convertible raise brought in roughly $484M net, retired the expensive Oxford
Finance secured loan in full, issued no stock, and leaves nothing to repay before 2032. For a
company burning about $52M a quarter — the accumulated deficit went from $448.9M at year-end
2025 to $501.7M at 31 March 2026 — that is a genuine de-risking. Cash after the raise is
roughly $625-640M against $500M of cheap convertible debt.

**On communication, they damaged themselves.** The launch-timing guidance landed on the
approval call itself, and the market had clearly assumed something faster. Stifel's analyst
called the late-third-quarter guidance "somewhat extended." The stock fell $19.54, or 17.6%,
to close at $91.51 on 15 July 2026. Within a week at least four plaintiffs' firms — Pomerantz,
Bragar Eagel & Squire, Kirby McInerney, and Bronstein Gewirtz & Grossman — opened
investigations into whether the company's earlier disclosures about launch readiness were
adequate.

To be clear about what that is and is not: these are law-firm investigations, not a filed
class action, and firms open them reflexively after any sharp single-day drop. They are not
evidence of wrongdoing. But they are evidence that the gap between what management let the
street assume and what management actually delivered was wide enough to look actionable. That
is a mark against expectation-management, and it is the second such mark this year — the June
mutated-gene readout also came in below what the company's own earlier trial had conditioned
investors to expect.

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — VERIFIED? NO.

This is the most important finding in the dossier, and it is a negative one.

The board entry for this name carries a downside floor of $60. **I cannot verify that as a
floor.** A floor, in this book, means something that mechanically catches the price: a deal
price a buyer is contractually obliged to pay, a cash balance, a court-supervised recovery, a
contingent-value right (a contractual payment tied to a later milestone). Celcuity has none of
those.

What it has is cash of roughly $625-640M against $500M of convertible debt — net cash of about
$140M, or roughly $3 a share against a $82.27 price, on about 48.8 million shares. That is the
only hard number on the balance sheet, and it is nowhere near $60.

The $60 figure is therefore a modelled bear case, not a backstop, and the model has to work
hard to get there. At $60 the equity is worth about $2.93B and the enterprise about $2.79B.
For that to be conservative you already have to assume the launch broadly works — peak annual
sales somewhere north of $1.2B, valued at a little over two times peak sales. If the launch
genuinely stumbles, if the tolerability profile caps real-world uptake, or if oncologists
default to the weaker two-drug regimen, peak sales of $600-800M would put the same multiple
around $30-40 a share.

My honest read on a defensible adverse value is **$50-55**, and even that is an estimate
rather than a floor. Below it there is nothing structural until you approach net cash. An
investor sizing this position should treat the downside as open, not bounded.

## 5. RED FLAGS

- **Tolerability is a commercial problem, not just a safety line.** Mouth sores affected 72% of
  patients on the three-drug regimen and 58% on the two-drug regimen, severe in 22% and 12%
  respectively. Patients need a preventive steroid mouthwash. Rash hit 30-40%. Raised blood
  sugar hit 46-57%, though severe cases were rare at under 2%. Real-world oncology practice is
  far less tolerant of daily management burden than a trial protocol is, and Reuters
  specifically flagged tolerability alongside the launch delay as the reason the stock fell.
- **The launch date has already slipped once and can slip again.** "Late" third quarter is five
  to nine weeks away and depends on a first-time commercial company building drug supply. A
  slip into the fourth quarter would be the second broken expectation in a quarter.
- **Four law-firm investigations opened inside nine days** — an overhang on management
  credibility even if nothing is ever filed.
- **One product, one indication, one pathway.** There is no second business to fall back on.
- **Competition is arriving in the population they want next.** The supplemental filing targets
  patients with a PIK3CA mutation — a market that already has alpelisib and capivasertib, and
  where Relay Therapeutics' zovegalisib won Breakthrough Therapy designation on 3 February 2026
  and is running a Phase 3 trial against capivasertib. The label expansion is not into empty
  space.
- **The dilution is deferred, not avoided.** The $500M convertible becomes shares if the stock
  recovers past its conversion price.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

- **Full approval, not accelerated** — no confirmatory-trial condition, no withdrawal risk.
- **A genuine white space.** Roughly 37,000 U.S. patients a year with this cancer lack a PIK3CA
  mutation and until 14 July 2026 had no targeted option in this pathway at all. This is the
  first and only approved drug covering all four class I PI3K enzymes plus both mTOR complexes.
- **The head-to-head data is real.** Against alpelisib in the mutated-gene group, gedatolisib
  delivered 11.1 and 11.3 months versus 5.6, with response rates of 48.9% and 35.7% versus
  26.0%, and dramatically less high blood sugar — 11.5-15.0% versus 57.9% — with fewer patients
  stopping for side effects (2.6-3.8% versus 7.1%). On the specific side effect that has held
  this drug class back commercially, Celcuity's drug is the better-behaved one.
- **Funded through the launch.** No maturity before 2032, no equity issued, expensive secured
  debt retired.
- **The street has not abandoned it.** The consensus price target is $155.11 with a median of
  $157, a high of $178 and a low of $110 — every published target sits above the current price.
  H.C. Wainwright moved to $155, Citizens to $177, Stifel held $175, all after the approval.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The pattern worth noticing is that Celcuity has now released three pieces of objectively good
news in a row — a head-to-head win, a fully funded balance sheet, an early approval — and the
stock has fallen on all three. That is what a crowded, fully-anticipated position looks like as
it unwinds. The buyers who were there for the decision have been paid and have left. The buyers
who need to show up next are the ones who buy commercial-stage oncology companies on quarterly
prescription trends, and they will not commit before they see a revenue line. There is a real
gap between those two shareholder bases, and the stock has to cross it without a catalyst.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

**The single most important thing to weigh: this seat was bought for a dated regulatory
decision; that decision fired favourably on 14 July 2026; and the position is nonetheless
down. The event thesis is closed. What remains is an execution story with an unverified
floor.**

Those are two different investments, and the second one does not belong in an event-driven
